rules.title: Security deposit capped at 1.5 months' rent
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld.
rules.key_value: 1.5 months' rent (max 2.5 months total at lease start including first month's rent)

coverage.summary: Most residential rental properties, including mobile homes. Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant makes a written request, which brings the tenancy under the law 30 days later.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Seasonal rentals of 125 days or less (for the deposit-investment rules)

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant requests coverage in writing (coverage applies 30 days after the request).
rules.penalty: Tenant may recover double the amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). Unlawful use of deposit funds is a disorderly persons offense (N.J.S.A. 46:8-25).
rules.quoted_span: The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act: good cause required to evict or refuse to renew
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent.
rules.key_value: Listed good cause required; relocation for illegal occupancy = 6x monthly rent

coverage.summary: Most residential rentals, including single-family homes, apartment buildings, mobile homes and mobile home park lots, and rooming and boarding homes. Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units (owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings) are excluded.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest house occupants
Units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies the unit

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-unit premises with two or fewer rental units; transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest house guests (unless they reside there continually and have no other residence); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member.
rules.penalty: If the landlord evicts for personal occupancy and does not occupy the unit for 6 months, or evicts to retire the property and then uses it residentially within 5 years, the landlord is liable for treble damages plus attorney fees, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for the retirement case (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6).
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause. The landlord must be able to prove in court that he has grounds for an eviction.

rules.title: No statewide rent cap; increases must not be unconscionable and must comply with local rent control
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.
rules.key_value: No state cap; increase must not be unconscionable

coverage.summary: Residential tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act. Local rent control ordinances, where a municipality has adopted one, set the actual limits.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: HUD-owned or HUD-subsidized housing and NJHMFA-financed projects are not subject to municipal rent control

rules.quoted_span: The increase in rent must not be unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
rules.interaction: The state does not control rents; municipalities may adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances, which are enforced by local boards. Rent increases must comply with those ordinances.

rules.title: Newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years
rules.requirement: If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered.
rules.key_value: 30-year exemption from local rent control after completion of construction

coverage.summary: Newly constructed multiple dwellings, for 30 years following completion of construction.

rules.quoted_span: Under the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law ( N.J.S.A. 2A:42 -84.5), newly constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction of the building.
rules.interaction: This state law overrides municipal rent control ordinances for newly constructed multiple dwellings during the 30-year period.
rules.conflict_note: State exemption limits the reach of local rent control ordinances. The guide does not state the statute's procedural conditions, such as filing requirements before construction, which a reviewer should check.

rules.title: No rent increases to cover condominium or cooperative conversion costs
rules.requirement: If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities.

coverage.summary: All tenants in buildings converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, regardless of protected tenancy status.
required_facts_not_in_data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership

rules.quoted_span: If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination bars source-of-income discrimination
rules.requirement: A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income protected; penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense

coverage.summary: All landlord-tenant relationships, except two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and single-sex residences.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single-family home
Residences exclusively for one sex (e.g., YMCA)

rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex.
rules.penalty: Fines and penalties of up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a)), plus possible damages and an order to rent the unit to the complainant.
rules.quoted_span: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

notes: Source is the NJ DCA Truth in Renting guide (official summary). The guide says landlords may charge the cost of a credit report and 'reasonable rental application fees' but cites no state fee cap or statute, so no application_screening_fees record was extracted. The guide does not mention criminal-history screening limits (Fair Chance in Housing Act) or algorithmic rent setting. Quoted spans had line breaks normalized to single spaces. Relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy evictions is folded into the just-cause record.
